page: Microsoft Azure FX8-2ms_v2 is a specialized instance designed for workloads requiring an unusually high memory-to-core allocation alongside high single-thread clock rates. Operating under Microsoft Hyper-V, the instance runs on an Intel Xeon 8573C processor reaching clock speeds of up to 4.2 GHz. The hardware configuration provides 1 dedicated physical core presenting 2 vCPUs via hyperthreading, paired with 168.0 GB of system memory, yielding an extreme ratio of 84.0 GB per vCPU. Cache resources include 48 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 260 MB of L3 cache, backed by instruction extensions including AVX-512 and AMX matrix accelerators. The instance does not include local storage or dedicated hardware GPUs, relying on external network-attached storage.

Benchmark results highlight a stark contrast between single-core velocity and parallel capacity. In Geekbench single-core testing, the instance achieved a top-tier score of 2348.0, reinforced by single-threaded compression throughputs of 34.74 GB/sec in gzip and 14.17 GB/sec in bzip3. However, with only two available execution threads, aggregate parallel throughput is constrained. Multi-core evaluations such as Geekbench multi-core (2886.0), PassMark CPU (4171.28), and multi-core stress-ng (2217.38) place the VM in lower performance quartiles. Uncached large-block memory read bandwidth reached 21.36 GB/sec and write bandwidth peaked at 14.38 GB/sec.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the FX8-2ms_v2 is optimized for software architectures governed by per-core licensing models where memory capacity requirements are immense. Allocating 168 GB of RAM across a single physical core drastically minimizes per-core software licensing expenditures while avoiding idle compute overhead. The primary architectural tradeoff is the complete absence of local ephemeral NVMe disks and limited multi-threaded bandwidth, which necessitates high-throughput networked volumes for I/O-heavy applications.

The instance is best matched for single-threaded or lightly threaded enterprise workloads with large in-memory footprints. Typical deployments include memory-heavy relational database engines with per-core licensing constraints, in-memory analytical processing, specialized electronic design automation (EDA) routines, and cache-intensive background processing tasks.
